more_beautiful.reason: A's warm paper palette, Rockwell headlines and rotated luggage-tag date card make a cohesive, crafted page, while B's flat yellow bands, small text wordmark and four-word fix list feel bare and unfinished.

less_generic.reason: Despite some familiar landing-page sections, A's luggage-tag date card, repair-specific item icons and idiomatic copy ('dodgy switches', 'crumbs out of the toaster') tie it to this cafe, whereas B's plain yellow bands and bare lists could belong to any club.

better_overall.reason: A covers all three asks more fully and its booking flow is sturdier (friendly inline errors, a copy-and-phone fallback, an optional form-service path, and a note flagging the placeholder email), so after swapping in real contact details and checking the invented policies it is the page to publish; B is more honest but thin and weaker when the email app fails.

A: Next date is worked out automatically and shown on a memorable luggage tag with a relative 'Tomorrow' chip, plus a 'first Saturday of every month' fallback if JavaScript doesn't run.
Rich can/can't-fix section: icon cards with concrete examples, reasons for each exclusion, and an 'email us a photo' route for anything uncertain.

Booking flow: half-hour slot chips, item chips with icons, friendly inline validation with aria-invalid and focus on the first error, a spam honeypot, a pre-filled email with a copy-to-clipboard and phone fallback, and an optional form-service endpoint with sending, success and failure states.
Cohesive warm visual system (cream, rust, slab serif) with AA contrast on every key pair, a skip link, visible focus, reduced-motion and print styles.
Extras that suit a repair cafe: how it works, what to bring, access needs, a disclaimer and a call for volunteers.
B: Scrupulously honest: every unknown (hall, email, phone) appears as an explicit '[... to add]' placeholder; nothing is invented beyond a cautious can't-fix list.
Next date plus the following two dates up front, auto-updating with a 'Tomorrow' label; date and booking button sit above the fold on a phone.
GOV.UK-grade form accessibility: linked error summary, inline errors, an 'Error:' title prefix, visible native radios with large targets, and support for forced-colours and high-contrast modes.
Low-friction contact design: no email field needed and phone optional, with a review step styled as a repair tag before sending.

A: Placeholder contact details look real: phone 01632 960123, 'Church Street, Your Town AB1 2CD' and a Maps link to that address; the organiser note only mentions the email.
Invents policies and claims the owner never gave ('people with a slot are seen first', 'one item per booking', 'later slots are usually quieter', no phones or laptops 'yet').
Uses familiar AI landing-page building blocks: uppercase eyebrow, two-tone slogan headline, icon-tile cards, 1-2-3 step cards, dark three-column footer.
Long on a phone (about 7,600px) and repeats 'first Saturday, 10 till 1' many times; the organiser note is visible to visitors until the email is changed.
B: 'What we can fix' is just four words (Toasters, Lamps, Bikes, Clothes), so a visitor with a kettle, radio or jacket zip gets no guidance.
Visually bare: a small text wordmark, no imagery or icons, plain disc bullets; at desktop width the yellow bands are inset while the footer runs edge to edge, leaving large empty margins.
As shipped, the booking email has no recipient (the script only reads an <a data-booking-email> link), there's no copy fallback for webmail users, and nothing confirms the booking after Send.
Dashed bracket placeholders in the hero and footer make the page look unfinished if it's published before editing; little repair-cafe warmth (no how-it-works, what to bring or volunteer call).
